claim: Adjunctive dexamethasone reduces mortality from tuberculous meningitis (TBM) but not disability.
source: Adjunctive dexamethasone reduces mortality from tuberculous meningitis (TBM) but not disability, which is associated with brain infarction.
evidence: This is a statement in the abstract that references established knowledge about dexamethasone treatment for TBM.

claim: Disability from tuberculous meningitis is associated with brain infarction.
source: Adjunctive dexamethasone reduces mortality from tuberculous meningitis (TBM) but not disability, which is associated with brain infarction.
evidence: This statement is made in the abstract and is supported by citations in the introduction.

claim: Aspirin prevents TBM-related brain infarction through its anti-thrombotic, anti-inflammatory, and pro-resolution properties.
source: We hypothesised that aspirin prevents TBM-related brain infarction through its anti-thrombotic, anti-inflammatory, and pro-resolution properties.
evidence: This is the stated hypothesis of the study, based on known properties of aspirin.

claim: 41 participants were randomised to placebo, 39 to aspirin 81 mg/day, and 40 to aspirin 1000 mg/day between October 2014 and May 2016.
source: 41 participants were randomised to placebo, 39 to aspirin 81 mg/day, and 40 to aspirin 1000 mg/day between October 2014 and May 2016.
evidence: This is a direct statement of the trial enrollment data.

claim: TBM was proven microbiologically in 92/120 (76.7%) participants.
source: TBM was proven microbiologically in 92/120 (76.7%) and baseline brain imaging revealed ≥1 infarct in 40/114 (35.1%) participants.
evidence: This is a direct statement of diagnostic data from the trial.

claim: Baseline brain imaging revealed ≥1 infarct in 40/114 (35.1%) participants.
source: TBM was proven microbiologically in 92/120 (76.7%) and baseline brain imaging revealed ≥1 infarct in 40/114 (35.1%) participants.
evidence: This is a direct statement of imaging data from the trial.

claim: The primary safety outcome occurred in 5/36 (13.9%) given placebo, and in 8/35 (22.9%) and 8/40 (20.0%) given 81 mg and 1000 mg aspirin, respectively (p=0.59).
source: The primary safety outcome occurred in 5/36 (13.9%) given placebo, and in 8/35 (22.9%) and 8/40 (20.0%) given 81 mg and 1000 mg aspirin, respectively (p=0.59).
evidence: This is a direct statement of the primary safety outcome results.

claim: The primary efficacy outcome occurred in 11/38 (28.9%) given placebo, 8/36 (22.2%) given aspirin 81 mg, and 6/38 (15.8%) given 1000 mg aspirin (p=0.40).
source: The primary efficacy outcome occurred in 11/38 (28.9%) given placebo, 8/36 (22.2%) given aspirin 81 mg, and 6/38 (15.8%) given 1000 mg aspirin (p=0.40).
evidence: This is a direct statement of the primary efficacy outcome results.

claim: Planned subgroup analysis showed a significant interaction between aspirin treatment effect and diagnostic category (Pheterogeneity = 0.01).
source: Planned subgroup analysis showed a significant interaction between aspirin treatment effect and diagnostic category (Pheterogeneity = 0.01) and suggested a potential reduction in new infarcts and deaths by day 60 in the aspirin treated participants with microbiologically confirmed TBM (11/32 (34.4%) events in placebo vs. 4/27 (14.8%) in aspirin 81 mg vs. 3/28 (10.7%) in aspirin 1000 mg; p=0.06).
evidence: This is a direct statement of subgroup analysis results.

claim: Aspirin treatment suggested a potential reduction in new infarcts and deaths by day 60 in participants with microbiologically confirmed TBM (11/32 (34.4%) events in placebo vs. 4/27 (14.8%) in aspirin 81 mg vs. 3/28 (10.7%) in aspirin 1000 mg; p=0.06).
source: Planned subgroup analysis showed a significant interaction between aspirin treatment effect and diagnostic category (Pheterogeneity = 0.01) and suggested a potential reduction in new infarcts and deaths by day 60 in the aspirin treated participants with microbiologically confirmed TBM (11/32 (34.4%) events in placebo vs. 4/27 (14.8%) in aspirin 81 mg vs. 3/28 (10.7%) in aspirin 1000 mg; p=0.06).
evidence: This is a direct statement of subgroup analysis results.

claim: CSF analysis demonstrated aspirin dose-dependent inhibition of thromboxane A2.
source: CSF analysis demonstrated aspirin dose-dependent inhibition of thromboxane A2 and upregulation of pro-resolving CSF protectins.
evidence: This is a direct statement of CSF analysis results.

claim: CSF analysis demonstrated aspirin dose-dependent upregulation of pro-resolving CSF protectins.
source: CSF analysis demonstrated aspirin dose-dependent inhibition of thromboxane A2 and upregulation of pro-resolving CSF protectins.
evidence: This is a direct statement of CSF analysis results.

claim: The addition of aspirin to dexamethasone may improve outcomes from TBM and warrants investigation in a large phase 3 trial.
source: The addition of aspirin to dexamethasone may improve outcomes from TBM and warrants investigation in a large phase 3 trial.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the trial results.

claim: Tuberculous meningitis kills or disables around half of sufferers.
source: New host-directed therapies are urgently required for all forms of tuberculosis, but especially for tuberculous meningitis (TBM), the most lethal form of the disease, which kills or disables around half of sufferers (Thwaites, 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Thwaites, 2013.

claim: Attempts to optimise bacteria-directed anti-tuberculosis regimens have not been shown to clearly benefit patients with TBM.
source: To date, attempts to optimise bacteria-directed anti-tuberculosis regimens have not been shown to clearly benefit patients with TBM (Ruslami et al., 2013; Heemskerk et al., 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Ruslami et al., 2013 and Heemskerk et al., 2016.

claim: Host-directed therapy with adjunctive anti-inflammatory corticosteroids has been shown to reduce mortality from TBM, although without reduced disability amongst survivors.
source: In contrast, host-directed therapy with adjunctive anti-inflammatory corticosteroids has been shown to reduce mortality from TBM, although without reduced disability amongst survivors (Prasad et al., 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Prasad et al., 2016.

claim: Cerebral infarction is the commonest cause of irreversible neurological injury from TBM.
source: Cerebral infarction is the commonest cause of irreversible neurological injury from TBM (Lammie et al., 2009).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Lammie et al., 2009.

claim: TBM-related infarcts are typically located in the territories of the proximal middle cerebral artery and the medial lenticulostriate and thalamoperforating vessels, where the basal meningeal inflammatory exudate is most intense.
source: TBM-related infarcts are typically located in the territories of the proximal middle cerebral artery and the medial lenticulostriate and thalamoperforating vessels, where the basal meningeal inflammatory exudate is most intense (Lammie et al., 2009; Hektoen, 1896; Misra et al., 2011).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Lammie et al., 2009; Hektoen, 1896; and Misra et al., 2011.

claim: Some autopsy studies have either failed to find arterial thrombosis associated with infarcts, or found it to be uncommon.
source: Some autopsy studies have either failed to find arterial thrombosis associated with infarcts, or found it to be uncommon (Doniach, 1949); whereas others have reported that thrombosis is common, especially when associated with tuberculous vasculitis (Poltera, 1977).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Doniach, 1949.

claim: Some autopsy studies have reported that thrombosis is common, especially when associated with tuberculous vasculitis.
source: Some autopsy studies have either failed to find arterial thrombosis associated with infarcts, or found it to be uncommon (Doniach, 1949); whereas others have reported that thrombosis is common, especially when associated with tuberculous vasculitis (Poltera, 1977).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Poltera, 1977.

claim: TBM-related infarcts are caused by a combination of vasospasm, intimal proliferation, and thrombosis.
source: The limited available evidence suggests that TBM-related infarcts are caused by a combination of vasospasm, intimal proliferation, and thrombosis (Lammie et al., 2009).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Lammie et al., 2009.

claim: Aspirin acts by irreversibly inhibiting the cyclooxygenase pathway of arachidonic acid metabolism and the production of prostanoids.
source: Aspirin acts by irreversibly inhibiting the cyclooxygenase pathway of arachidonic acid metabolism and the production of prostanoids (Vane, 1971).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Vane, 1971.

claim: Low dose aspirin (75–150 mg) prevents ischaemic cerebrovascular disease.
source: Low dose aspirin (75–150 mg) prevents ischaemic cerebrovascular disease (Richman and Owens, 2017) and higher dose aspirin (up to four grams daily) is used for the treatment of some inflammatory conditions (e.g. rheumatic fever) (Cilliers et al., 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Richman and Owens, 2017.

claim: Higher dose aspirin (up to four grams daily) is used for the treatment of some inflammatory conditions (e.g. rheumatic fever).
source: Low dose aspirin (75–150 mg) prevents ischaemic cerebrovascular disease (Richman and Owens, 2017) and higher dose aspirin (up to four grams daily) is used for the treatment of some inflammatory conditions (e.g. rheumatic fever) (Cilliers et al., 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Cilliers et al., 2015.

claim: Aspirin's anti-inflammatory effects are thought to occur at doses >600 mg daily, through the inhibition of pro-inflammatory prostaglandins (e.g. PGE2, PGF2α and PGD2) and the unstable prostanoid, thromboxane A2 (TXA2).
source: Its anti-inflammatory effects are thought to occur at doses >600 mg daily, through the inhibition of pro-inflammatory prostaglandins (e.g. PGE2, PGF2α and PGD2) and the unstable prostanoid, thromboxane A2 (TXA2) (Botting, 2010).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Botting, 2010.

claim: Low dose aspirin causes less inhibition of pro-inflammatory prostaglandins, but causes clinically significant inhibition of TXA2 and platelet aggregation.
source: Low dose aspirin causes less inhibition of pro-inflammatory prostaglandins, but causes clinically significant inhibition of TXA2 and platelet aggregation.
evidence: This is a statement about the mechanism of action of low-dose aspirin based on established knowledge.

claim: The inhibitory effect on platelets and thrombus formation was thought to explain aspirin's well-documented reduction in the risk of death from stroke and myocardial infarction.
source: Until recently, the inhibitory effect on platelets and thrombus formation was thought to explain aspirin's well-documented reduction in the risk of death from stroke and myocardial infarction (Raju et al., 2011).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Raju et al., 2011.

claim: Aspirin's effects may be augmented by its ability to trigger the production of 15-epi-lipoxins, 17R-resolvins and protectins, molecules that alongside the recently discovered maresins actively promote the resolution of inflammation.
source: However, these effects may be augmented by aspirin's ability to trigger the production of 15-epi-lipoxins, 17R-resolvins and protectins, molecules that alongside the recently discovered maresins actively promote the resolution of inflammation (Spite and Serhan, 2010).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Spite and Serhan, 2010.

claim: The 'pro-resolution' properties of aspirin are not shared with any other non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAID), or corticosteroids.
source: The 'pro-resolution' properties of aspirin are not shared with any other non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAID), or corticosteroids.
evidence: This is a statement about the unique properties of aspirin based on established knowledge.

claim: There are data from murine models of tuberculosis which suggest aspirin and other non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs may enhance Mycobacterium tuberculosis killing.
source: Furthermore, there are intriguing data from murine models of tuberculosis which suggest aspirin and other non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs may enhance Mycobacterium tuberculosis killing (Byrne et al., 2007; Vilaplana et al., 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Byrne et al., 2007 and Vilaplana et al., 2013.

claim: A previous trial randomised 118 Indian adults with TBM to standard anti-tuberculosis chemotherapy, with or without aspirin (150 mg daily).
source: The first randomised 118 Indian adults with TBM to standard anti-tuberculosis chemotherapy, with or without aspirin (150 mg daily) (Misra et al., 2010).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Misra et al., 2010.

claim: In a previous trial, by 3 months, brain magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) proven infarction occurred in 13 (43%) in the placebo arm and 8 (24%) in the aspirin group (p=0.18).
source: By 3 months, brain magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) proven infarction occurred in 13 (43%) in the placebo arm and 8 (24%) in the aspirin group (p=0.18).
evidence: This statement describes results from a previous trial cited as Misra et al., 2010.

claim: In a previous trial, aspirin was associated with a reduction in mortality (43% versus 22%, p=0.02) without a significant increase in adverse events.
source: Aspirin was associated with a reduction in mortality (43% versus 22%, p=0.02) without a significant increase in adverse events.
evidence: This statement describes results from a previous trial cited as Misra et al., 2010.

claim: A second trial randomised 146 South African children with TBM to standard anti-tuberculosis chemotherapy plus placebo (n = 50), low-dose aspirin (75 mg/day) (n = 47), or high-dose aspirin (100 mg/kg/day) (n = 49).
source: The second trial randomised 146 South African children with TBM to standard anti-tuberculosis chemotherapy plus placebo (n = 50), low-dose aspirin (75 mg/day) (n = 47), or high-dose aspirin (100 mg/kg/day) (n = 49) (Schoeman et al., 2011).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Schoeman et al., 2011.

claim: In a previous trial in South African children, aspirin had no significant impact on survival, motor or cognitive outcomes.
source: Aspirin had no significant impact on survival, motor or cognitive outcomes.
evidence: This statement describes results from a previous trial cited as Schoeman et al., 2011.

claim: Between October 2014 and May 2016, 192 patients were assessed for eligibility and 120 were randomised.
source: Between October 2014 and May 2016, 192 patients were assessed for eligibility and 120 were randomised (Figure 1 and supplementary file 2): 41 received placebo, 39 received aspirin 81 mg/day, and 40 received aspirin 1000 mg/day.
evidence: This is a direct statement of trial enrollment data, also shown in Figure 1.

claim: Two participants in the placebo group were lost to follow-up after 57 and 217 days, respectively.
source: Two participants in the placebo group were lost to follow-up after 57 and 217 days, respectively.
evidence: This is a direct statement of trial follow-up data.

claim: Gastro-intestinal bleeding event data were missing for seven participants (three placebo, 4 aspirin 81 mg) because they either died or were lost to follow-up before day 60.
source: Gastro-intestinal bleeding event data were missing for seven participants (three placebo, 4 aspirin 81 mg) because they either died or were lost to follow-up before day 60.
evidence: This is a direct statement of missing data in the trial.

claim: MRI-proven new intracranial bleeding event or infarct data were missing for 15 subjects (six placebo, 7 Aspirin 81 mg, 2 Aspirin 1000 mg) because they either died, were lost to follow-up before day 60, or they were too unwell to have scans within 60 ± 10 days.
source: MRI-proven new intracranial bleeding event or infarct data were missing for 15 subjects (six placebo, 7 Aspirin 81 mg, 2 Aspirin 1000 mg) because they either died (four placebo, 6 aspirin 81 mg, 1 aspirin 1000 mg), were lost to follow-up before day 60 (1 placebo), or they were too unwell to have scans within 60 ± 10 days (two placebo, 1 aspirin 81 mg, 2 aspirin 1000 mg).
evidence: This is a direct statement of missing data in the trial.

claim: The per-protocol population excluded 22 participants: two had a confirmed alternative diagnosis, one had confirmed MDR TBM, and 19 received <30 days of study drug for reasons other than death.
source: The per-protocol population excluded 22 participants (Figure 1): two had a confirmed alternative diagnosis (Listeria monocytogenes meningitis and Mycobacterium avium intracellulare meningitis), one had confirmed MDR TBM, and 19 received <30 days of study drug for reasons other than death (five placebo; 8 aspirin 81 mg; 9 aspirin 1000 mg).
evidence: This is a direct statement of per-protocol population definition, also shown in Figure 1.

claim: The predominant gender was male (65.8%).
source: The predominant gender was male (65.8%), the median age was 41 years and duration of illness was 10 days.
evidence: This is a direct statement of baseline characteristics.

claim: The median age was 41 years.
source: The predominant gender was male (65.8%), the median age was 41 years and duration of illness was 10 days.
evidence: This is a direct statement of baseline characteristics.

claim: The median duration of illness was 10 days.
source: The predominant gender was male (65.8%), the median age was 41 years and duration of illness was 10 days.
evidence: This is a direct statement of baseline characteristics.

claim: Most participants had mild to moderate illness severity, with only 15 (12.5%) MRC grade III at enrollment.
source: Most participants had mild to moderate illness severity, with only 15 (12.5%) MRC grade III at enrollment.
evidence: This is a direct statement of baseline disease severity.

claim: The placebo and aspirin 1000 mg groups had a higher proportion with infarcts (42.5% and 38.5% respectively) than the aspirin 81 mg group (22.9%).
source: Baseline MRI revealed ≥1 infarct in 40/114 (35.1%) participants; the placebo and aspirin 1000 mg groups had a higher proportion with infarcts (42.5% and 38.5% respectively) than the aspirin 81 mg group (22.9%).
evidence: This is a direct statement of baseline imaging data.

claim: According to the published diagnostic criteria 92/120 (76.7%) had definite TBM, 17/120 (14.2%) probable, and 9/120 (7.5%) possible TBM.
source: According to the published diagnostic criteria 92/120 (76.7%) had definite TBM, 17/120 (14.2%) probable, and 9/120 (7.5%) possible TBM (Marais et al., 2010).
evidence: This is a direct statement of diagnostic categorization using published criteria.

claim: Of the 92 participants with definite TBM, 42 (45.7%) had M. tuberculosis cultured from the CSF and acid-fast bacilli were seen in the CSF in 50 others (54.3%).
source: Of the 92 participants with definite TBM, 42 (45.7%) had M. tuberculosis cultured from the CSF and acid-fast bacilli were seen in the CSF in 50 others (54.3%).
evidence: This is a direct statement of microbiological diagnostic data.

claim: Amongst patients with culture-confirmed disease, 10/42 (23.8%) had isoniazid resistant infection and one (2.4%) had MDR TBM.
source: Amongst patients with culture-confirmed disease, 10/42 (23.8%) had isoniazid resistant infection and one (2.4%) had MDR TBM.
evidence: This is a direct statement of drug susceptibility data.

claim: Only one new cerebral bleed occurred (in the aspirin 81 mg group): an asymptomatic micro-haemorrhagic transformation of a lacunar infarct.
source: Only one new cerebral bleed occurred (in the aspirin 81 mg group): an asymptomatic micro-haemorrhagic transformation of a lacunar infarct.
evidence: This is a direct statement of safety outcome data.

claim: Four gastro-intestinal bleeding events were defined as either serious, or grade 3 or 4: two serious haematemesis events in the placebo group and one in the aspirin 81 mg group, and one grade 3 episode of melena in the aspirin 1000 mg.
source: Four gastro-intestinal bleeding events were defined as either serious, or grade 3 or 4: two serious haematemesis events in the placebo group and one in the aspirin 81 mg group, and one grade 3 episode of melena in the aspirin 1000 mg.
evidence: This is a direct statement of safety outcome data.

claim: The majority of bleeding events (16/20; 80%) were defined as either grade 1 or two events, 15/16 described as >5 mls of changed or fresh blood aspirated from a nasogastric tube, and 1 episode of melena.
source: The majority of bleeding events (16/20; 80%) were defined as either grade 1 or two events, 15/16 described as >5 mls of changed or fresh blood aspirated from a nasogastric tube, and 1 episode of melena (supplementary file 3).
evidence: This is a direct statement of safety outcome data.

claim: None of the bleeding events required active management, but on each occasion the study drug was stopped immediately.
source: None of these events required active management, but on each occasion the study drug was stopped immediately.
evidence: This is a direct statement of how bleeding events were managed.

claim: The observed risk of a new MRI-proven brain infarction was lower in the aspirin treated patients compared to placebo, although not statistically significant (p=0.18).
source: The observed risk of a new MRI-proven brain infarction was lower in the aspirin treated patients compared to placebo, although not statistically significant (p=0.18) (Table 2).
evidence: This is a direct statement of efficacy outcome data.

claim: 9/15 (60.0%) of brain infarcts seen at baseline in the aspirin 1000 mg group resolved by day 60, whereas resolution only occurred in 1/7 (14.2%) in the aspirin 81 mg group and 6/14 (42.9%) in the placebo group (p=0.14).
source: In addition, 9/15 (60.0%) of brain infarcts seen at baseline in the aspirin 1000 mg group resolved by day 60, whereas resolution only occurred in 1/7 (14.2%) in the aspirin 81 mg group and 6/14 (42.9%) in the placebo group (p=0.14).
evidence: This is a direct statement of imaging outcome data.

claim: There was only one death in the aspirin 1000 mg treated participants by day 60.
source: There was only one death in the aspirin 1000 mg treated participants by day 60.
evidence: This is a direct statement of mortality data.

claim: In the per-protocol population new infarction or death occurred by day 60 in 19/95 (20.0%): 10/34 (29.4%) given placebo, 6/31 (19.3%) given aspirin 81 mg, and 3/30 (10.0%) given 1000 mg aspirin (p=0.16).
source: In the per-protocol population new infarction or death occurred by day 60 in 19/95 (20.0%): 10/34 (29.4%) given placebo, 6/31 (19.3%) given aspirin 81 mg, and 3/30 (10.0%) given 1000 mg aspirin (p=0.16) (Table 3).
evidence: This is a direct statement of per-protocol efficacy outcome data.

claim: In the per-protocol population, the observed absolute risk reductions in the aspirin 81 mg and aspirin 1000 mg groups versus placebo were −10.1% (95% CI −29.7% to +11.0%) and −19.4% (95% CI −37.4% to +0.6%), respectively (p=0.16).
source: The observed absolute risk reductions in the aspirin 81 mg and aspirin 1000 mg groups versus placebo were −10.1% (95% CI −29.7% to +11.0%) and −19.4% (95% CI −37.4% to +0.6%), respectively (p=0.16).
evidence: This is a direct statement of per-protocol efficacy outcome data.

claim: In the per-protocol population, no deaths occurred in the aspirin 1000 mg group, compared to 13% and 11% in the aspirin 81 mg and placebo groups respectively (p=0.11).
source: No deaths occurred in the aspirin 1000 mg group, compared to 13% and 11% in the aspirin 81 mg and placebo groups respectively (p=0.11).
evidence: This is a direct statement of per-protocol mortality data.

claim: No clear subgroup signal was seen for any subgrouping variable except for the diagnostic category which showed a significant interaction with the aspirin treatment effect (Pheterogeneity = 0.01).
source: No clear subgroup signal was seen for any subgrouping variable except for the diagnostic category which showed a significant interaction with the aspirin treatment effect (Pheterogeneity = 0.01) and suggested a potential reduction in new infarcts and deaths by day 60 in the aspirin-treated participants with microbiologically confirmed TBM (11/32 (34.4%) events in placebo vs. 4/27 (14.8%) in aspirin 81 mg vs. 3/28 1000 (10.7%) in aspirin 1000 mg; p=0.06).
evidence: This is a direct statement of subgroup analysis results.

claim: The beneficial effects of aspirin were most marked in the aspirin 1000 mg group (aspirin 81 mg vs placebo: odds ratio (OR) 0.33, 95% CI 0.09–1.20, p=0.093; aspirin 1000 mg vs. placebo: OR 0.23, 95% CI 0.06–0.93, p=0.039).
source: These beneficial effects were most marked in the aspirin 1000 mg group (aspirin 81 mg vs placebo: odds ratio (OR) 0.33, 95% CI 0.09–1.20, p=0.093; aspirin 1000 mg vs. placebo: OR 0.23, 95% CI 0.06–0.93, p=0.039) (Figure 2).
evidence: This is a direct statement of subgroup analysis results, also shown in Figure 2.

claim: The number-needed-to-treat (NNT) to prevent an infarct or death by day 60 was 5 for aspirin 81 mg and 4 for aspirin 1000 mg.
source: These effects equate to the number-needed-to-treat (NNT) to prevent an infarct or death by day 60 of 5 for aspirin 81 mg and 4 for aspirin 1000 mg.
evidence: This is a calculation based on the subgroup analysis results.

claim: In the ITT population there was no significant difference in death or disability by day 60 or month eight across the treatment groups.
source: In the ITT population there was no significant difference in death or disability by day 60 or month eight across the treatment groups (Table 5).
evidence: This is a direct statement of secondary outcome data.

claim: The 8-month mortality was 14/118 (11.9%): 5/39 (12.8%) in the placebo group versus 6/39 (15.4%) and 3/40 (7.5%) in the 81 mg and 1000 mg aspirin groups respectively (p=0.50).
source: The 8-month mortality was 14/118 (11.9%): 5/39 (12.8%) in the placebo group versus 6/39 (15.4%) and 3/40 (7.5%) in the 81 mg and 1000 mg aspirin groups respectively (p=0.50; Figure 2 panels).
evidence: This is a direct statement of mortality data, also shown in Figure 2.

claim: In the per-protocol population, there was a trend to better 8 month outcomes in the aspirin 1000 mg group (p=0.13).
source: In the per-protocol population, however, there was a trend to better 8 month outcomes in the aspirin 1000 mg group (p=0.13)(Table 5).
evidence: This is a direct statement of per-protocol secondary outcome data.

claim: Aspirin at either dose was not associated with a significant reduction in hospital stay (median 32 days for each group; p=0.84).
source: Aspirin at either dose was not associated with a significant reduction in hospital stay (median 32 days for each group; p=0.84).
evidence: This is a direct statement of secondary outcome data.

claim: Hydrocephalus was less common by day 60 in the aspirin 1000 mg group (2/38 (5.3%)) than the aspirin 81 mg (5/32 (15.6%)) and placebo groups (8/35 (22.9%)(p=0.09).
source: Hydrocephalus, however, was less common by day 60 in the aspirin 1000 mg group (2/38 (5.3%)) than the aspirin 81 mg (5/32 (15.6%)) and placebo groups (8/35 (22.9%)(p=0.09).
evidence: This is a direct statement of imaging outcome data.

claim: None of the participants in the trial with hydrocephalus underwent ventriculoperitoneal shunting.
source: None of the participants in the trial with hydrocephalus underwent ventriculoperitoneal shunting.
evidence: This is a direct statement of clinical management data.

claim: Overall, aspirin was not associated with a significant increase in grade 3 or four or serious adverse events, with the possible exception of more cardiac events in the aspirin groups (p=0.08).
source: Overall, aspirin was not associated with a significant increase in grade 3 or four or serious adverse events, with the possible exception of more cardiac events in the aspirin groups (p=0.08) (Table 6).
evidence: This is a direct statement of adverse event data.

claim: The numbers of participants with ≥1 serious adverse event were 12 (29.3%) in the placebo arm, 15 (38.5%) in the aspirin 81 mg arm and 9 (22.5%) in the 1000 mg arm (p=0.31).
source: The numbers of participants with ≥1 serious adverse event were 12 (29.3%) in the placebo arm, 15 (38.5%) in the aspirin 81 mg arm and 9 (22.5%) in the 1000 mg arm (p=0.31).
evidence: This is a direct statement of adverse event data.

claim: Adverse events resulting in study drug stop or interruption occurred in 7 (17.1%) given placebo, 10 (25.6%) 81 mg aspirin, and 10 (25.0%) 1000 mg aspirin (p=0.56).
source: Adverse events resulting in study drug stop or interruption occurred in 7 (17.1%) given placebo, 10 (25.6%) 81 mg aspirin, and 10 (25.0%) 1000 mg aspirin (p=0.56).
evidence: This is a direct statement of adverse event data.

claim: Hyponatraemia (plasma sodium <125 mmol/L) was more common in those treated with placebo (33 (80.5%)) than aspirin 81 mg (24 (61.5%)) or 1000 mg (25 (62.5%)) (p=0.11).
source: Hyponatraemia (plasma sodium <125 mmol/L) was more common in those treated with placebo (33 (80.5%)) than aspirin 81 mg (24 (61.5%)) or 1000 mg (25 (62.5%)) (p=0.11).
evidence: This is a direct statement of adverse event data.

claim: Partial least squared discriminant analysis 2-dimensional score plot of CSF taken from all surviving participants 30 days from randomization showed clustering of lipid mediators according to treatment group suggesting dose-dependent effects.
source: Partial least squared discriminant analysis 2-dimensional score plot of CSF taken from all surviving participants 30 days from randomization showed clustering of lipid mediators according to treatment group suggesting dose-dependent effects (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is a direct statement of CSF analysis results, also shown in Figure 3A.

claim: In participants who received >30 days of study drug, comparison of baseline with day 30 CSF found dose-dependent inhibition of TXB2 (the stable metabolite of TXA2) and up-regulation of pro-resolving protectins, with significant differences observed in the aspirin 1000 mg group compared to placebo.
source: Furthermore, in those participants who received >30 days of study drug we compared baseline with day 30 CSF and found dose-dependent inhibition of TXB2 (the stable metabolite of TXA2) and up-regulation of pro-resolving protectins, with significant differences observed in the aspirin 1000 mg group compared to placebo (Figure 3B; supplementary file 6).
evidence: This is a direct statement of CSF analysis results, also shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The trial was not powered to show an impact on longer term survival or neurodisability.
source: The trial was not powered to show an impact on longer term survival or neurodisability and therefore does not provide definitive, practice-changing evidence that adjunctive aspirin improves outcomes in all adults with TBM.
evidence: This is a statement about the trial design and limitations.

claim: The findings support the hypothesis that aspirin has effects on tuberculosis-associated neuro-inflammation that are independent of dexamethasone and may lead to additional improvements in clinical outcomes.
source: However, the findings support the hypothesis that aspirin has effects on tuberculosis-associated neuro-inflammation that are independent of dexamethasone and may lead to additional improvements in clinical outcomes.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the trial results.

claim: The serial brain images support the assertion that aspirin's benefit may be driven by the upregulation of pro-resolving molecules: 60% of infarcts seen at baseline had resolved by day 60 in the aspirin 1000 mg group compared with 14.2% in the aspirin 81 mg group and 42.9% in the placebo group.
source: The serial brain images also support the assertion that aspirin's benefit may be driven by the upregulation of these pro-resolving molecules: 60% of infarcts seen at baseline had resolved by day 60 in the aspirin 1000 mg group compared with 14.2% in the aspirin 81 mg group and 42.9% in the placebo group.
evidence: This is an interpretation of imaging data to support a mechanistic hypothesis.

claim: This phase two randomised placebo-controlled trial suggests that daily aspirin 81 mg or 1000 mg can be given safely with dexamethasone and anti-tuberculosis drugs for the treatment of HIV-uninfected adults with TBM.
source: In summary, this phase two randomised placebo-controlled trial suggests that daily aspirin 81 mg or 1000 mg can be given safely with dexamethasone and anti-tuberculosis drugs for the treatment of HIV-uninfected adults with TBM.
